messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raymond is a 71-year-old married man who has worked as a security guard for the better part of two decades, a role he took on after retirement from an earlier career and one that, until recently, gave him a clear sense of purpose. Approximately eight months ago, Raymond was on duty at a public venue when a terrorist attack unfolded in the space he was responsible for protecting. The attack was sudden and chaotic — there were people running, screaming, the smell of smoke, and Raymond found himself unable to reach several individuals who were injured in the initial blast. He was not physically wounded, but he was close enough to witness the immediate aftermath in visceral detail: faces, sounds, the particular quality of the light through the haze. He survived. Others did not fare as well. And it is that gap — between what he was there to do and what he was able to do — that has sat at the centre of his suffering ever since.

In the weeks following the attack, Raymond began to notice that his memories of the event were both overwhelming and strangely fractured. He can recall specific images with almost painful clarity — a particular face, the angle of a doorway, the sound of an alarm — yet when he tries to assemble these fragments into a coherent account, even for himself, the story falls apart. He cannot tell it from beginning to end. The sequence dissolves. On other occasions, he finds himself recounting what happened with a flat, detached quality, as though narrating something that happened to a stranger rather than to him — a dissociation that leaves him unsettled in its own way, as though even his own experience has become inaccessible.

What has come to dominate Raymond's waking life, however, is a set of beliefs about himself that have hardened into convictions. He is certain that another man — a more competent man, a real security professional — would not have found himself in that position, or would have responded differently. He has failed, he believes, in the role that mattered most to him: the role of protector. These appraisals have not remained passive. They have driven him toward a vigilance that is now relentless. He arrives at any room — the break room at work, a restaurant with his wife, a waiting area at a clinic — and immediately positions himself with his back against a wall, scanning every face, every entrance, cataloguing who is present and who might be dangerous. It is not a choice he makes consciously anymore; it is what his body does before his mind catches up. And alongside this physical hypervigilance, he spends hours in a kind of grinding mental rehearsal — not processing the event, but turning over fantasies of retribution, imagining confrontations with those responsible, calculating what he should have done and what he might yet do. He has come to believe that if he can just think it through completely enough, he will find the answer that restores something of what he has lost.

The tragedy of this pattern is that it does the opposite. The constant scanning and the rumination keep Raymond's nervous system primed and his attention fixed on threat, and this sustained state of arousal makes it harder, not easier, to process what happened. The fragmented, non-sequential quality of his memories persists — perhaps deepens — because the mental space required to integrate experience is crowded out by the endless cycle of vigilance and revenge fantasy. And the very strategies he uses to manage his sense of failure end up confirming it: the wall-sitting, the scanning, the inability to relax in any public space, all of it reads to him as evidence that he is broken in a way that cannot be repaired. His wife has noticed the change. Dinners out have stopped. Conversations have grown shorter. She has told him, gently and then less gently, that she no longer recognises the man she married.

Raymond presented for treatment after his supervisor raised concerns about his performance at work — the hypervigilance that once seemed like professional attentiveness had become conspicuous and disruptive. What he fears most is that the assessment will confirm what he already suspects: that he is beyond help. What he hopes, in a quieter register, is that someone will tell him he is wrong.
